explanations.explanation: That's the one. The song says, "We give thanks to You, O God; we give thanks, for Your Name is near." (Psalm 75:1) The thanks comes with its reason attached. When I thank my oven, I just pat it and hope for the best.

Enemies running off would be a fine reason for a song, but this verse never mentions it. The reason it gives is "for Your Name is near." (Psalm 75:1) Nobody is running anywhere in that line. Our heads love to add a plot twist the song never wrote.

explanations.answer: Because the harvest came in full
explanations.explanation: A full harvest would give anybody a reason to sing, friend. But Psalm 75:1 doesn't mention one. The reason it gives for the thanks is "for Your Name is near." I read that verse twice looking for a harvest, and it just isn't in there.

Close, but the people don't hold the calendar. The voice says, "When I choose a time, I will judge fairly." (Psalm 75:2) The choosing belongs to the one speaking. I once tried to pick my own bake time by opening the oven every two minutes, and the cookies and I both learned something.

You caught it. The voice says, "When I choose a time, I will judge fairly." (Psalm 75:2) The one speaking picks the time, and the verse doesn't hand that choice to the people. No ballot box in sight, friend.

Yes! The voice says, "it is I who bear up its pillars." (Psalm 75:3) Everybody else is quaking, and this voice is the one holding the pillars. I get nervous when my cooling rack wobbles, so I'm impressed.

Roaring seas sound dramatic, but they don't show up in this verse. What the voice says is that when the earth and all its dwellers quake, "it is I who bear up its pillars." (Psalm 75:3) The picture here is about pillars, not water. I'd say the seas can stay out of this one.

That's a big, grand answer, but Psalm 75:3 doesn't say it. The verse says that when the earth and all its dwellers quake, "it is I who bear up its pillars." The voice holds things up, and no gates get opened. Sometimes the plain answer is the one holding the pillars.
That's it. The voice says to the proud, "Do not boast." (Psalm 75:4) Boasting is the whole problem in that line. I've bragged about my mustache to an empty bakery, so I know how easy it is to start.

Worry is a fair guess, since a quaking earth would make anybody nervous. But the voice says to the proud, "Do not boast." (Psalm 75:4) The warning is aimed at the proud, and worry isn't what it names.
I'm an expert wanderer, friend, mostly toward the cookie dough. But that isn't what the voice says to the proud. It says, "Do not boast." (Psalm 75:4)

Right on target. The voice says, "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck." (Psalm 75:5) That's a big thing to lift a horn against. I can't even win an argument with my own oven timer.

Neighbors can be a handful, I'll admit. But the verse names something else: "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck." (Psalm 75:5) The warning points up, not next door.

The temple is a natural guess, but it isn't named here. The voice says, "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck." (Psalm 75:5) Heaven is the word in the verse. Hold onto that one, friend.

You've got it. The song says exaltation comes neither from east nor west nor out of the desert, "but it is God who judges." (Psalm 75:6-7) The song lists three places it doesn't come from, then points to who it does come from. That's a good way to teach: clear the wrong spots first, then say the right one.

An army looks like it should be in charge, especially one with a drum section. But the song says exaltation doesn't come from east, west or the desert, and then it says, "but it is God who judges." (Psalm 75:6-7) An army isn't in that line at all.

explanations.answer: From the kings of the earth
explanations.explanation: Kings feel like a safe guess, since they have the crowns. But the song says exaltation doesn't come from east, west or the desert, "but it is God who judges." (Psalm 75:6-7) The song names God here, not kings.

Yes, that's the first blank. The song says, "He brings down one and exalts another." (Psalm 75:7) Down is the word for the first one. I know a thing or two about being brought down, since I once went face-first into the chocolate chips.
Yes, that fills the second blank. The song says, "He brings down one and exalts another." (Psalm 75:7) One gets brought down, and the other gets lifted up. Exalts is the word that finishes the line.
Spares sounds gentle, but it isn't the word in the verse. The song says, "He brings down one and exalts another." (Psalm 75:7) That's the pair: down for the first, exalts for the second.
Scatters is a lively word, and I use it a lot with sprinkles. But Psalm 75:7 doesn't use it. The verse says, "He brings down one and exalts another."

Back is a tricky one, friend. "Brings back" sounds like a real phrase, but it's not this verse. The song says, "He brings down one and exalts another." (Psalm 75:7) It's the little word down that goes in the first blank.

That's the word. The song says, "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." (Psalm 75:8) The cup is in the hand of the LORD, and the wicked are the ones who drink from it. That's a sobering verse, so I'll keep my apron on and say it plainly.

Priests are a natural guess, but they aren't in this verse. It says the LORD pours from His cup, "and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." (Psalm 75:8) Wicked is the word that fits the blank.
Kings is a big, important-sounding word, but it isn't the one here. The verse says, "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." (Psalm 75:8) Wicked is the word in the blank.

That sounds like a quick taste, but the verse says otherwise. "All the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." (Psalm 75:8) Dregs means all the way to the bottom. A sip and a set-down is not what this verse describes.

Correct, it's False. The verse says, "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." (Psalm 75:8) They drink it down to the bottom of the cup, not one little sip. When I say I'll have just one cookie, my track record looks better than that cup.

It's True. After the cup, the singer says, "But I will proclaim Him forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob." (Psalm 75:9) The song turns from the heavy cup back to praise. And I like that it says forever.

The verse says the opposite, friend. The singer says, "But I will proclaim Him forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob." (Psalm 75:9) So it's True. The singer says forever, not just for a little while.

explanations.answer: Wicked horns cut off and righteous horns exalted
explanations.explanation: That's the ending. The voice says, "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted." (Psalm 75:10) The horns that were lifted high in verses 4 and 5 come back in the last line. The song closes the circle, and I always like a song that remembers where it started.

explanations.answer: Wicked horns exalted and righteous horns cut off
explanations.explanation: You've got the two pieces, but they're swapped. The verse says, "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted." (Psalm 75:10) The wicked ones get cut off, and the righteous ones get lifted up. Same thing happens when I put the salt in the sugar jar: right ingredients, wrong places.

explanations.answer: Both kinds of horns cut off alike
explanations.explanation: That would make it an even-handed ending, but the song splits them. The voice says, "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted." (Psalm 75:10) Only the wicked horns are cut off. The righteous ones are the ones that get lifted.
